practice1.prompt: trace the loop with a debug print, then fix the total

cases.name: the three numbers add up to 6

hiddenCases.name: works for any list of numbers
the trace shows every pass through the loop
hiddenCases.describe: a debug line for each pass through the loop, as well as the result

hiddenCases.name: the accumulation happens in a loop
hiddenCases.describe: a for loop that builds the total up

practice1.hint: Two separate things are being asked for. The debug print goes inside the loop and stays there, so three numbers produce three trace lines before the answer. The bug is on the line that assigns to running -- read what your own trace prints and it names itself.

questions.prompt: Why put the debug print inside the loop rather than after it?
choices: Outside the loop you see one value; inside it you see the sequence, which is where the bug is
Python only allows prints inside loops
questions.explain: The final value tells you the answer is wrong, which you already knew. The sequence tells you it was being replaced rather than added to, which is the bug itself.

questions.prompt: What makes a debug print useful rather than noise?
choices: It names the variable it is showing
It is marked so you can find and remove it later
It prints on every iteration when the bug is about a sequence
It prints as much of the program state as possible
questions.explain: A labelled, findable, well-placed print answers one question. Dumping everything produces output nobody reads, which is the same as no print at all.

questions.prompt: The trace shows running as 1, then 2, then 3. What does that tell you?
choices: The loop runs too many times
running is being assigned each item rather than having each item added to it
The list is in the wrong order
questions.explain: A running total would show 1, then 3, then 6. Seeing the input values themselves come back means the assignment replaced the total instead of growing it.

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of print debugging compared with a debugger?
choices: You have to decide in advance what to print, and change the code to change your mind
It only works on small programs
It cannot be used inside functions
questions.explain: A debugger lets you look at anything once you are stopped. A print commits you to a guess about what mattered, and asking a different question means editing and re-running.

reflection-exercise1.hint: A print answers one of two questions: what is in this variable, or did the program get here at all. Say which you would use and when.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Placement is the whole skill. Say where the print goes relative to the part you suspect, and why there rather than somewhere else.
